slides.title: Chapter 4: Keys and Addresses
slides.say: Chapter 3 gave you the node; chapter 4 gives you ownership: one secret number, the curve that hides it, and the address formats that carry it in public. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4.
slides.concept: From a secret number to the string you can safely read out loud

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: the key, its public face, its travel clothes, its addresses, and the habits - every claim arrives with its receipt, and one slide is signed by Satoshi's own source comment. A question to think about is this: which part do you expect to be hardest? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in every section.
slides.concept: Five parts - from one secret number to safe habits

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: These are the questions the chapter answers, from how a private key becomes a public key to where its printed statements differ from the standards and from a run of Bitcoin Core 31.1. Each is taken up in turn on the slides that follow. If you can answer them, chapter 4 is yours.
slides.concept: If you can answer these, chapter 4 is yours

slides.title: One chapter, five branches
slides.say: This branch of the chapter starts from a payment. Alice wants to pay Bob, but the thousands of full nodes that will verify her transaction do not know who Alice or Bob are, and the design is meant to keep it that way, to protect their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Keys, Format and Address.
slides.concept: Five branches - every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Keys
slides.say: This branch of the chapter starts from a payment. Alice wants to pay Bob, but the thousands of full nodes that will verify her transaction do not know who Alice or Bob are, and the design is meant to keep it that way, to protect their privacy (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Keys.
slides.concept: A number, a curve, and a one-way multiplication

slides.title: The 1976 paper that split the key in two
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 1976-11. In November 1976 two Stanford researchers published 'New Directions in Cryptography', opening with a sentence that aged well: 'We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.' Their idea - a key split into a public half and a private half, tied by a one-way computation - is the exact machinery this chapter runs: multiply a point, publish the result, keep the multiplier. The source is Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), November 1976; ACM A.M. Turing Award 2015.
slides.concept: Public and private halves - one 1976 idea under every address

slides.title: A private key is just a number
slides.say: A private key is simply a number, picked at random. Control over the private key is the root of user control over all funds associated with the corresponding public key: the key is used to create the signatures that spend bitcoins by proving control of the funds used in a transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why is a password a bad private key even if it is long? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Private key and Entropy.
slides.concept: Any 256-bit number - the hard part is choosing it unpredictably

slides.title: The curve everyone agreed on
slides.say: The name secp256k1 identifies the specific elliptic curve and the set of constants that Bitcoin uses. The curve is y squared = x cubed + 7 over a finite field of prime order p, with p = 2 to the 256 minus 2 to the 32 minus 2 to the 9 minus 2 to the 8 minus 2 to the 7 minus 2 to the 6 minus 2 to the 4 minus 1 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Secp256k1 and Generator point.
slides.concept: secp256k1: two primes, one base point, shared by all

slides.title: Double-and-add: the one-way street
slides.say: Elliptic curve multiplication takes a point P and a whole number k and produces kP, which is defined as P + P + P + ... + P with k terms. A question to think about is this: where exactly does 'easy forward, hard backward' live in these 13 lines? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Point multiplication and Discrete logarithm.
slides.concept: 256 doublings forward - and no known road back

slides.title: Prove the key without showing it
slides.say: A digital signature is a number that a signer computes from a message and from a private key. Anyone who has the message, the signature and the matching public key can verify the signature, that is, can check that it was produced by the holder of the private key and that the message has not been altered since. A question to think about is this: what would 'showing the key' even mean here? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Digital signature and Key control proof.
slides.concept: Chapter 1's house key, kept honest: sign, never reveal

slides.title: Formats
slides.say: This branch is about writing the same information down in different ways. A private key, a public key and a hash commitment are all numbers, and a number can be shown in binary, in hexadecimal, in a compact alphabet with a built-in checksum, or in a two-dimensional barcode. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Format.
slides.concept: The same numbers, dressed to travel

slides.title: Why 58? Satoshi left the reasons in the file
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2009-2010. Open src/base58.h in the source tree this course pins and the first thing after the copyright lines - 'Copyright (c) 2009-2010 Satoshi Nakamoto' - is a design memo. Why base-58 and not base-64? The source is src/base58.h at the corpus-pinned commit 05bc2f53 of bitcoin/bitcoin: the copyright line naming Satoshi Nakamoto (2009-2010) and the 'Why base-58 instead of standard base-64' comment, quoted verbatim on the slide (MIT).
slides.concept: The address alphabet is usability engineering, documented

slides.title: From key to WIF and back
slides.say: The wallet import format, abbreviated WIF, is the text form in which a private key is exported from one wallet and imported into another. It is the base58check encoding of the version byte 0x80 followed by the 32-byte private key, and, for keys that produce compressed public keys, an extra byte 01 at the end (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think about this case: decode a WIF by eye: which characters can never appear? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Wallet import format and Compressed private key.
slides.concept: WIF is the same number, dressed for transport

slides.title: The checksum that catches your typo
slides.say: A checksum is a short value derived from a piece of data and attached to it. Anyone who has the data and the attached value can recompute the check and see whether they still agree; if the data was altered, they will with overwhelming probability disagree. A question to think about is this: what does the checksum NOT protect you from? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Checksum and Base58Check.
slides.concept: Four bytes stop a mistyped address from costing coins

slides.title: Addresses
slides.say: This branch turns the keys of the first branch into something one person can hand to another. An address is a short string that a receiver gives to a payer so that the payer's wallet can build a transaction output that only the receiver can spend. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Address.
slides.concept: Commitments you can read out loud

slides.title: From public key to address, exactly
slides.say: A pay to public key hash address, abbreviated P2PKH, is the legacy address in which the output script commits to the HASH160 of the receiver's public key. The output script is OP_DUP OP_HASH160 <commitment> OP_EQUALVERIFY OP_CHECKSIG and the spender's input script is the signature followed by the public key (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why hash the key at all? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in P2pkh address and Hash160.
slides.concept: Two hashes and an alphabet - the pipeline, executed

slides.title: The address that eats coins
slides.say: This is a true story, dated since 2011; balance fetched 2026-10-06. Spell a message inside an address, append a valid checksum, and you get 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE - a perfectly valid address whose matching key nobody has, because it was chosen as text, not derived from a key. People send coins to it anyway: at this build it held 13.41747849 BTC across 5,832 deposits, and not one satoshi has ever left. The source is blockstream.info API, address 1BitcoinEaterAddressDontSendf59kuE, fetched 2026-10-06 during this build: funded 1,341,747,849 sat over 5,832 outputs, spent 0 - the figures pinned in EATER below.
slides.concept: An address commits to a key - it cannot conjure one

slides.title: SegWit and bech32: the second alphabet
slides.say: Segregated witness, or segwit, is an upgrade that moves signatures and scripts into a separate structure called the witness, committed to blocks apart from the tree of transactions (Lombrozo et al., 2015). The witness holds the data needed to check that a transaction is valid, but not the data that decides what the transaction does. Bech32 gives these outputs an alphabet without look-alike characters, so reading an address aloud no longer invites the old mistakes. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Segwit upgrade and Bech32Address.
slides.concept: New addresses move the witness and drop the look-alikes

slides.title: Error detection, measured
slides.say: Error detection is the property of a format that lets software notice that a string has been altered by an accident, such as a mistyped character. A question to think about is this: why does 'provably catches' beat 'has never missed so far'? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Error detection and Bch code.
slides.concept: bech32m catches what base58 provably misses

slides.title: Taproot, and what wallets do today
slides.say: Pay to taproot, abbreviated P2TR, is the output kind of segwit version 1. For a P2TR output the witness program is a point on the secp256k1 curve. A question to think about is this: which prefix will your first wallet hand you? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in P2tr and Default address type.
slides.concept: A real wallet's defaults, read from the node

slides.title: Practice
slides.say: This branch asks what a user or a developer should do with the material of the earlier branches today. The chapter ends with advanced keys and addresses, vanity addresses and paper wallets, and it surrounds them with remarks about how practice has changed since the first Bitcoin software. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Practice.
slides.concept: Habits that keep keys safe

slides.title: Habits the chapter prescribes
slides.say: Address reuse is the practice of receiving more than one payment to the same address. Because all the transactions are public, every payment to an address is visible together with every other payment to it. Think about this case: if one seed makes every address, what single thing must you back up? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Address reuse and Deterministic wallet.
slides.concept: Fresh address every time; the wallet derives, you back up once

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.say: Five lines, one per part; the agenda names the slides that prove each. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in every section.
slides.concept: If a line feels unproven, its part's slides carry the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything here is free. Open the eater address tonight and watch nothing move, because that standstill is this chapter's whole lesson about commitments. Ask yourself who could explain to a parent why bc1p addresses beat old 1-addresses for reading aloud. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 4, in Practice.
slides.concept: One secret number; everything else on these slides is derivation
